INITIAL BRIEF OF INTERVENOR JOHN DURLAND (AUTHORIZED
REPRESENTATIVE FOR TOM LATHAM)

I. Introduction and Summary of Position

Intervenor John Durland, acting as the Authorized Representative for Tom Latham,

submits this Initial Brief to support the approval of the Applicants' Route 894. Route 894

is the lowest-cost route that holds habitable structures to 85 or fewer, satisfies the

Commission's two highest-weighted routing factors, and presents no grid reliability

concerns, while every alternative trades a high-weight advantage for a low-weight one1.

For these reasons, Intervenor Latham respectfully requests that the Administrative Law

Judges recommend the approval of Route 894.




1
 Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews, Item 4332; Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of Will
McAdams, Item 5052.
 II. Application of Law: Route 894 Should Be Approved

A. Cost Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(E), the Commission must weigh the lowering of

cost to consumers2. Route 894 has an estimated base transmission line cost of

$1,680,919,000.3 As expert witness Brian C. Andrews established, the Commission

historically gives the greatest weight to estimated cost and absolute habitable structure

impacts, specifically noting this precedent in Docket No. 30168. Route 894 is the

lowest-cost option among the routes that hold habitable structures to 85 or fewer,

offering the most prudent financial path for Texas ratepayers4.



B. Habitable structures The Commission's policy of prudent avoidance under 16 TAC

§ 25.101(b)(3)(B) requires minimizing the exposure of populated areas to transmission

line infrastructure. Habitable structure count is the second primary routing factor

consistently evaluated with the highest weight by the Commission5. Route 894

successfully protects community values by impacting only 85 habitable structures within

500 feet of its centerline6. This figure ranks in the superior performance band across the

field of 122 filed routes.



C. Land use, parks, and viewshed Under PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC §

25.101(b)(3)(B), the Commission must consider the impact of a route on community

values, recreational and park areas, and historical and aesthetic values. Route 894

entirely avoids utilizing Links J11 and J26. Link J11 places high-voltage infrastructure

 within the immediate foreground visual zone of Colorado Bend State Park, and Link J26

directly abuts the boundary of Post Oak Ridge State Park7. By utilizing Link J27 instead,

Route 894 places zero miles of right-of-way within the defined foreground visual zone of

either state park8.



D. Engineering feasibility and reliability Route 894 is feasible from an engineering

perspective and presents no single point of failure or reliability concern. The

Commission must consider grid reliability and security when routing a new transmission

line9. Route 894 successfully navigates the flood-prone San Saba River by crossing it

perpendicularly and immediately moving to higher, more stable ground10. It minimizes

interaction with the San Saba River and Colorado River to a combined 5.14 miles,

actively avoiding the vulnerability associated with paralleling existing critical

infrastructure in areas known for unpredictable flash flooding.



E. Latham's specific stake Tom Latham is a direct descendant of the original settlers

who founded the Latham Ranch in San Saba County in 1865. The property has been

continuously owned and operated as a working ranch by his family for over 150 years.

The ranch relies strictly on agricultural operations, specifically cattle and goats, and

contains a ranch house that serves as a primary residence. Route 894 appropriately

avoids this localized concentration of impacts and protects a six-generation homestead.

 III. Application of Law: The Alternatives Do Not Displace 894

The alternative proposals, including any route using j6, including Route 296, Route 572,

and Route CCG, each carry certain advantages in low-weight routing factors11. None of

these alternatives overcomes the superior performance of Route 894 on the

highest-weighted factors of cost and habitable structures.



A. Comparative summary: Every alternative route that is less expensive than Route

894 impacts a higher number of habitable structures, and the only two routes with fewer

habitable structures cost approximately $45 million more12. Furthermore, the contested

alternatives fail to match Route 894's balance. Route CCG costs $1,754,606,644 and

impacts 105 structures13. Route 572 costs $1,689,249,000 and impacts 107 structures.

Route 296 costs $1,684,563,000 and impacts 105 structures. Route 739, a

representative route containing J6, costs $1,741,982,000 and impacts 129 structures14.



B. Route CCG specifically: While Route CCG reflects genuine landowner preferences

and the evidentiary record credits it on lower-weighted factors such as avoiding Rocky

Creek and Texas fatmucket (a freshwater mussel) habitat, clearing fewer acres of

fragmentation-sensitive habitat, and paralleling more existing compatible right-of-way, it

loses on the primary, dispositive factors of cost and habitable structures15. Additionally,

grid reliability considerations under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) counsel against Route

CCG because it takes a non-forward-progressing detour that requires 44.5 miles of
11
   Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews, Item 4332.
12
   Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews, Item 4332
13
   Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of Will McAdams, Item 5052.
14
   ONCOR AMENDED COMBINED DATA TABLE, Item 5985
15
   Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews, Item 4332
 transmission line to cover a direct distance of only 31.9 miles, ultimately crossing the

flood-prone San Saba River directly parallel to an existing 138-kV line to create an

unnecessary single point of failure.16 Furthermore, to manufacture its purported park

viewshed advantage against Route 894, Cherokee Creek Partners rely on expert

testimony that discards the Applicants’ standard 0.5-mile foreground visual zone and

arbitrarily expands the evaluation radius to 3 to 5 miles. The Commission should reject

this methodological gerrymandering. If an intervenor's expert is permitted to unilaterally

expand standardized metrics, such as the habitable structure radius or the 0.5-mile

visual zone, the entire CCN evaluation framework becomes untenable, destroying the

Commission’s ability to conduct an objective, apples-to-apples comparison of the filed

routes.



C. Remaining alternatives Routes utilizing Link J6, as well as Route 296 and Route

572, suffer from the same structural failure to balance the Commission's primary criteria.

Route 572 increases grid resiliency risks by crossing and paralleling the San Saba and

Colorado rivers for 11.59 miles, compared to Route 894's 5.14 miles17. Route 296

unnecessarily exposes 20 additional homes and businesses to the transmission line.

The routes containing J6, such as Route 739, would impose over $60 million in

unnecessary costs on Texas consumers while impacting significantly more habitable

structures18.




16
   Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of Will McAdams, Item 5052
17
   Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of Will McAdams, Item 5052
18
   ONCOR AMENDED COMBINED DATA TABLE, Item 5985
 IV. Conclusion and Request for Relief

Route 894 best satisfies the statutory factors as historically weighted by the

Commission. It offers the lowest cost while minimizing habitable structure impacts,

avoids severe reliability risks, and protects community and historical values. Intervenor

John Durland respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges recommend the

approval of Route 894.



Respectfully submitted,
/s/ John Durland Authorized Representative for Tom Latham
